rows: Employers and people controlling premises must assess and manage foreseeable legionella risks.
Any water system can support legionella growth where temperature, nutrients and stagnation are favourable.
Risk increases where systems create and disperse breathable water droplets.
A competent person should help identify and assess relevant water systems and exposure routes.
Controls can include temperature management, avoiding stagnation, cleaning and monitoring.
Written control arrangements and records may be needed for higher-risk systems.
Cooling towers and evaporative condensers require specific control and notification arrangements.
Control measures should be reviewed when systems, use, occupancy or monitoring results change.
A water system or cooling-tower record does not prove legionella growth or human exposure.
Premises-level conclusions require current system design, temperature, maintenance, sampling and aerosol evidence.
COSHH requires employers to prevent or adequately control exposure to wood dust.
Both hardwood and softwood dust can cause occupational asthma.
Hardwood dust is associated with a risk of nasal cancer.
Fixed local exhaust ventilation should capture dust at source where woodworking machinery generates it.
Extraction systems should be maintained and examined so they continue to perform effectively.
Dry sweeping and compressed-air cleaning can spread dust and should be replaced by safer methods.
Suitable respiratory protective equipment may be required for residual exposure and needs correct fit.
Health surveillance may be required where workers remain exposed to respiratory sensitisers.
The presence of woodworking or timber does not establish airborne concentration or control effectiveness.
Exposure conclusions require task, material, duration, extraction, cleaning, RPE and health-surveillance evidence.
COSHH requires exposure to metalworking fluids by inhalation, ingestion or skin contact to be prevented or controlled.
Metalworking-fluid mist can contribute to asthma and other respiratory disease.
Direct and repeated skin contact can cause dermatitis.
Enclosures and local exhaust ventilation should control mist generated by machining.
Fluid quality and bacterial contamination should be monitored and managed.
Skin exposure should be minimised through process controls, suitable gloves and hygiene.
Health surveillance is needed where exposure to fluid or mist remains.
Ill-health findings should trigger prompt investigation and review of control measures.
A machining process does not prove harmful exposure without evidence about mist, fluid condition and skin contact.
Risk depends on machine enclosure, extraction, fluid management, task duration, hygiene and worker susceptibility.
Employers must manage workplace temperature so workers are protected and reasonably comfortable.
There is no single statutory maximum working temperature because workplaces and activities differ.
Indoor workrooms should normally be at least 16°C, or 13°C where work involves rigorous physical effort.
Thermal risk assessment should consider air temperature, work rate, humidity, clothing and radiant heat.
Local heating, cooling, ventilation, work-rest arrangements and access to drinking water can reduce risk.
Heat stress can arise where the body cannot lose heat effectively.
PPE and heavy clothing can increase heat strain by limiting evaporation.
Controls should be reviewed during extreme weather and when processes or work patterns change.
An outdoor forecast or room thermometer reading alone does not determine whether work is safe.
Worker risk depends on duration, exertion, humidity, clothing, acclimatisation, health and available controls.
